summary:
How close can a swimming race be? In Baku, Azerbaijan, Cameron McEvoy reached the finish just four hundredths of a second ahead of his nearest rival.

The Australian swimmer won the men’s 50-metre freestyle on the opening night of the 2026 Swimming World Cup. His time was 20.22 seconds. Egor Kornev finished next in 20.26 seconds, and Sean Niewold took third in 20.82 seconds.

The winning time was also a new World Cup record. The previous mark, set by Josh Liendo last year, was 20.31 seconds. This was a record for the World Cup, not a newly announced world record.

McEvoy had another reason to smile. He said his previous personal best had stood for 11 years. He had not raced in a short-course event for several years, and he spoke about the long wait. A personal best is an athlete’s own fastest result.

He also said he would like to swim below 20 seconds. He did not reach that goal in this race: 20.22 is still above 20.

Baku is the first stop of the competition’s Silk Road Tour. For McEvoy, the opening race offered a win over other swimmers. His comments also showed that personal goals can remain important after a victory.
title: A Swim Decided by Four Hundredths of a Second
why_it_matters: The race shows how a close victory and personal goals can appear in the same sports story.
